lead: Pilotage is navigation by eye in the last mile, with no time for chartwork. Prepare it beforehand: what you will see and which line keeps you off the rocks.

sections.title: Work it out before you arrive

blocks.p: A **pilotage plan** is a card for the cockpit: each leg's heading, distance and minutes at your speed over the ground, what you will see at the turn and the danger beyond. Write bearings in degrees magnetic, as the compasses read; pilot books give them true, from seaward. At night use lit marks only.

fig.note: Running west, the church draws aft and its bearing rises

blocks.p: If a mark fails to appear on time, you may not be where you think: stop, fix, return to the last safe point. Where chart and pilot book disagree, assume the worse; if the book warns against today's wind, go elsewhere.
One person steers; the other navigates from the cockpit, calling headings and marks. The helm repeats each heading and reports when steady.

sections.title: Lines that keep you off the danger

blocks.p: Two charted objects in line make a **transit**: you are on that line whatever the plotter says. Pick objects far apart, and steer whatever heading holds them in line, bow into any cross-stream. Rear mark open (just out of line) to the left of the front one: you are left of the line, steer right.

fig.note: Rear light open to the left: you are left of the line

blocks.p: A **clearing bearing** is a limit, not a track: the bearing of a charted mark that just clears the danger, written NMT (not more than) or NLT (not less than). Up to it you may tack freely. A **back bearing** checks a mark astern: on track it reads the reciprocal of your course; if it creeps, you are being set.

fig.note: The shoal lies where the light bears more than 080°M

sections.title: Marks you must name at a glance

blocks.p: Lateral marks follow the **direction of buoyage**: in from the sea, or as the chart's arrow shows. Against it the sides swap. Region B reverses only the colours of lateral marks (red right returning); cardinals and all other marks are the same. A beacon stands on its danger: give it room.
At a fork, a lateral mark banded in the other colour, Fl(2+1), marks the **preferred channel**: for the main channel obey its main colour, so red with a green band stays to port in region A.

A cardinal is named for its safe side and flashes like a clock face; the long flash stops six being miscounted, and neighbours differ as Q and VQ. White Fl(2): isolated danger, under the mark. Iso, Oc, LFl 10s or Mo(A): safe water. Yellow: special mark, see the chart. Blue and yellow, Al Bu Y, racon D: new wreck.

sections.title: Naming a light, reading its colour

blocks.p: Time a light to name it. Oc is lit longer than dark, Iso half and half; Al changes colour on every bearing; VQ flashes twice a second. **Nominal range** assumes 10 miles of visibility, and a 3M pierhead light shows only close in. Against a town, stand off until both pierheads are certain: red to port, green to starboard. A narrow, half-lit entrance can wait for daylight.

fig.note: Which red is Fl R 5s? Time it before you commit

blocks.p: A **sectored light** changes colour with your bearing: white over the safe line, red and green either side, or red over a danger. Limits are true bearings from seaward: convert your compass bearing. Red on the way in usually puts you to port of the line: come to starboard. The edge flickers, and at 4 miles a 3° sector is two cables wide: keep to the middle.

fig.note: In the red: you are to port of the line, come to starboard

blocks.p: IALA **port traffic signals** are three lights, one above another. A yellow light beside the top exempts craft that can stay outside the main channel.

Three reds flashing: a serious emergency, stop or divert as told. A bridge has its own lights, given in the pilot book: commonly red and green mark the sides of the navigable span, white its centre. Ignore street lamps.

fig.note: Navigable span: under the white, between red and green

blocks.p: A plotter's chart can be tens of metres out and zooming adds no detail: marks in line beat the screen. Keep waypoints off the marks. 'Go to' draws a straight line from wherever you have drifted. At low speed COG wanders: steer by compass. Obey a virtual AIS mark like a buoy.

fig.note: Depths in metres below chart datum

blocks.p: On radar a **parallel index** line lies along your track at the planned passing distance: the echo should slide down it; if it comes inside, turn away. A VRM ring is a clearing range; the EBL, relative when head-up, marks a turn. For fog, note an echo's range and bearing for each turn.

In fog slow down, sound the signal, post a lookout and cross-check every aid. Without radar follow a **depth contour** as a handrail to a known mark: a steep, even one well outside the dangers. The sounder should read contour + tide − its own offset; less means you are inshore.

fig.note: Aim east of the entrance, then follow the 10 m line west

blocks.p: **Aim off**: steer deliberately to one side of the entrance, so that on finding the contour you know which way to turn. A fog signal says the mark is near, not where. Unsure of the next turn? Anchor and wait.
